# Notes Before the Survey Comes Back

*Written before the global engagement survey and before the real-estate committee reports, deliberately. A framework assembled after the survey is not a framework. It's a summary of what people said they wanted in the week they were asked, arranged to look like a decision.*

---

## What we're actually designing

The brief says remote work, office space, and collaboration tools. That's the visible layer, and it's the layer everyone in the industry is already fighting over in public. Days-per-week policies are announced, copied, and reversed within a quarter. Desk ratios are a spreadsheet. Tooling is a procurement cycle. None of it is difficult and none of it is ours.

What is not copyable in a quarter: the standard of writing our decisions are recorded in, the set of cities we can credibly hire in, the honesty of our promotion calibration, and the scheduling rights we've given to people who don't own a laptop. Those are slow, unglamorous, mostly invisible, and structurally hard for a competitor to reproduce by reading our careers page.

So I'd treat the location policy as necessary and visible — it's what candidates ask about, it's what the survey is equipped to measure, and it's how we demonstrate we've taken this seriously — and quietly spend the real effort on where decisions happen, who gets seen, and what we do about the half of the company for whom "flexibility" currently means nothing at all.

That ordering is the substance of these notes. Everything below is downstream of it.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

"Employees worldwide" is a phrase doing considerable hiding. I'm going to write as though we mean something specific: several tens of thousands of people, forty-plus countries, a knowledge-work core of perhaps 40% and a large remainder in plants, labs, field sales, retail and contact centres — with the executive committee and roughly two-thirds of promotion authority sitting in one or two home-market cities.

If that shape is wrong, this is the cheap moment to say so, because about a third of the specifics change and the rest holds. If it's *right*, then note what it implies: the loudest voices in this conversation are structurally the least representative of it, and the people with the most to gain from a genuine redesign are the ones least likely to be in the room where it's designed.

---

## What the survey can and can't tell us

"Employees want flexibility" is a finding I'd handle with some care. It's almost always true, everywhere, and it's a description of what people *say* rather than what they *do*. Stated preference for autonomy is close to universal. Revealed behaviour is that people come in on the day their manager comes in, and that a team's carefully negotiated hybrid charter dissolves in the first week of a genuine crisis. Enthusiasm for a new working model is trial appetite. Trial is easy. Repeat is the whole question.

The more useful line of enquiry — which I'd put to the people team as a suggestion rather than a correction — isn't *where would you prefer to work*. It's closer to: what did you do the last time something urgent broke at 4pm? Where were you physically when your last promotion was decided, and where was the person who decided it? Which meeting in your week would you pay money to not attend? What's the thing about your working life that's genuinely worse than it was three years ago, that you've stopped mentioning because you assume nobody can fix it?

Preference sells a policy. An inadequately served part of somebody's actual week buys a habit.

---

## Options, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd float all of these rather than propose any. Some are considerably more defensible than others, and I'd be interested in which ones people reach for unprompted, because that tells me something about the room I can't learn by asking.

**1. Overlap, not attendance — a bet on time as the real scarce resource.**
Stop legislating location and legislate synchronous overlap instead. Each team declares a band of three or four hours in which everyone is reachable, and owns everything outside it. Location then becomes a consequence rather than a rule, and it becomes a *team's* consequence. The interesting property is that this is enforceable, measurable and culturally neutral in a way "three days in the office" is not: it says nothing about whether you value presence, only that you owe your colleagues a predictable window. Cross-continental teams will discover the band is expensive. That discovery is useful — it's an org-design signal we currently pay for in attrition instead.

**2. Subsidiarity with an expiry date — a bet on the smallest unit that bears the cost.**
A thin global floor — non-negotiable, short enough to fit on one page — and everything above it decided by the team that lives with the consequences. The mechanism that matters isn't the delegation; it's the expiry. Every team arrangement lapses annually and must be re-argued. Arrangements that never have to be re-justified calcify into folklore within eighteen months, and folklore is what you're fighting when you try to change anything in year three.

**3. The office as instrument, not container — a bet on purpose-built rather than square metres.**
The office lost the desk argument and there's no point relitigating it. It has not lost the argument about rooms a home doesn't have: a room for a hard disagreement, a room for the first four weeks of somebody's career here, a bench, a kitchen, a wall you can cover in paper. That implies converting floor area rather than reducing it, and it implies a brutally honest metric — do people travel to this building voluntarily, without being told to? An office that only fills on mandate days has failed and is telling us so.

**4. The written record as infrastructure — a bet against tooling.**
Asynchronous work does not fail on software. It fails on prose. The scarce capability is the ability to write a decision memo that a colleague eleven time zones away can act on without a call, and that is a hiring criterion and a promotion criterion, not a platform purchase. One additional rule, which I'd want binding on the centre before anyone else: whichever channel the executive committee actually uses becomes the real headquarters, whatever the policy says. If decisions get made in corridors and ratified in documents, we don't have a distributed company, we have a distributed periphery.

**5. The non-laptop majority — a bet on fairness as an operating risk rather than a value.**
If flexibility turns out to be a benefit available only to people with a company laptop, we will have built a two-tier company and, worse, written it down. The currency for shift and field and plant work is different and mostly cheaper: control over the roster, the right to swap without a manager's approval, meaningful notice on schedule changes, compressed weeks, predictability. There's reasonable evidence that schedule control is worth more to a shift worker than home working is to an analyst. It's under-explored, hard for competitors to copy because it requires actually rebuilding scheduling systems, and nobody's marketing it. This may be the most valuable idea on the page and it will get the least airtime, which is roughly why I'd argue for it sideways rather than directly.

**6. Hiring geography as the moat — a bet that this is a talent strategy wearing a facilities costume.**
The durable asset here isn't employee satisfaction, which regresses to the market within two years. It's the administrative capability to employ excellent people in cities where we will never open a building — payroll, employer-of-record, mobility, tax, the craft of managing someone you haven't met. Slow, tedious, unglamorous, and precisely therefore not reproducible in a quarter by a competitor who announces a policy. Offered lightly, because it will sound like empire-building: the version of this project that matters in five years may be the one that changed who we can hire, not where we sit.

**7. An explicitly co-located tier, held loosely — a bet on segmentation.**
Some functions and some individuals genuinely perform better in a room every day, and in several of our markets an office life is not a cost to be minimised but the actual texture of a career. So keep a high-presence model available, named, and legitimate — not as punishment, not as default. Two or three units, no more, because it's a hedge rather than a strategy and because it's exactly the kind of idea that expands to fill whatever attention it's given. One condition, non-negotiable: it must not become the promotion track. If it does, everything else on this page is theatre.

---

## The constraint I'd design from, not to

Start from the calibration meeting. Whatever we publish, the true policy of this company is revealed by who got promoted last cycle and how physically close they were to the person who decided it. If proximity predicts advancement, then flexibility is a benefit that quietly costs money to accept, everyone works that out inside a year, and the policy dies of its own accord while remaining formally in force. That is the first line of the brief, not the last.

Two things I'd want somebody to own from week one rather than discover in month nine:

**Proximity bias, measured backwards before we change anything.** Pull the last two promotion cycles and correlate outcome with physical distance from the deciding manager, controlling for level and function. Do it now, so the baseline exists before we have a stake in the answer. It's an uncomfortable number and its discomfort is the point.

**Employment law, works councils, and permanent-establishment tax exposure.** Drawn once, early, quietly, by people who do this for a living — and treated as an external condition of entry rather than as a topic. German co-determination, Dutch and French statutory rights to request, the corporate-tax consequences of letting someone work from a country we have no entity in, data residency where our default tooling isn't reachable. A condition can be engineered around. A topic gets re-opened in month seven under time pressure by an executive who misses the atrium.

---

## What I'd do first

Not a global policy. A small, ugly, deliberately over-reaching test: five or six teams chosen for maximum spread — different countries, different functions, at least one that doesn't work at a desk — each running a *genuinely different* model, including two that our own leadership finds slightly wrong. One team with no office at all. One team required in a room four days a week and given the budget to make that worth it. One team whose only rule is the overlap band.

Run them through a real crunch period, not a calm quarter. Have someone physically present, watching, in more than one of them. Calm-month satisfaction is trial data and I wouldn't let it into the second meeting.

And I'd manufacture one argument on purpose. Put the no-office model in front of the country leadership in the market with the strongest presence norms and the real-estate committee in the same week, and watch how the disagreement resolves. If this whole process has been frictionless, we've learned nothing about which of these models anyone will defend when it becomes inconvenient.

---

## Tests fixed now, before the evidence arrives

Because criteria written afterwards are commentary.

Each model survives its own worst quarter without silently reverting. Reversion under pressure is the failure mode, not dissatisfaction.

There is at least one element per model that isn't a policy document — a room, a hiring geography, a writing standard, a scheduling right — that a competitor cannot reproduce inside a quarter by copying what we publish.

A new joiner in Manila can explain it to a parent in one clause, in their own language, without our help.

Something in it is worth having if you work a shift. If the answer to the non-laptop question is a wellbeing app, we've failed the test and should say so plainly.

Promotion rates at eighteen months are within tolerance across presence quartiles, controlling for level. This is the gate. Everything else is preference data.

At least two of the surviving models are ones we currently think are wrong.

---

The failure mode isn't choosing the wrong number of office days. It's that by month six the policy exists as a fact inside our own organisation — with a sponsor, a name, a slot in the plan, a change-management workstream — and the case for continuing has quietly become the case for not having wasted the year. At which point attendance becomes a reported metric, because it's the only thing that's easy to count, and we spend three years managing a proxy.

The defence isn't discipline. It's having kept a genuinely different operating model alive in parallel the whole way through, so that when the moment comes there's somewhere else to go and it doesn't have to be invented in a meeting.

We aren't choosing between a building and a spare bedroom. We're deciding where decisions actually get made, and who has to be in the room to be part of them — and we're competing for the best three hours of somebody's day against employers who currently have those hours and don't know they're at risk.
